hero.title: The competency framework for the creator era
hero.lead: CreaComp maps digital creative literacy: the body of knowledge that allows a person to critically receive, understand, imagine, make, publish and capitalise on content and projects in digital environments.

object.title: A framework for digital creative literacy
object.lead: Someone creating online draws on knowledge that several frameworks already describe, but separately. What is missing is not one more competence: it is the model that holds them together.
body: Creation has become a structuring dimension of digital environments. Recommendation algorithms, content production, generative artificial intelligence, digital entrepreneurship: people's capacity to understand these mechanisms and to produce value through them now conditions their economic, cultural and civic autonomy.

That capacity is not uncharted ground. DigComp describes the digital competence of citizens, EntreComp entrepreneurial competence, media and information literacy critical reception, and research on creativity the act of inventing. Each of these frameworks illuminates one side of it; none brings them together in a single model.

This is where CreaComp comes in: an integrated framework describing a person's capacity to understand digital environments, to create in them intentionally, to turn ideas into finished work, to engage with communities and to build lasting autonomy around what they make. It is built around a single question:
object.question: What is a person actually able to do in digital environments, and what value are they able to create there?

why.title: Value has moved
body: Generative artificial intelligence has collapsed the cost of production: a competent text, a clean visual, an edited video are becoming universally accessible. What becomes ordinary loses its value, and value moves towards both ends of the creative chain.

That displacement is what justifies the architecture of the framework: the eye and the relationship weigh as much as making itself. Existing frameworks describe one end or the other; CreaComp holds both in a single model, with the same grammar of levels and the same evidence of assessment.

framework.title: The whole framework at a glance
framework.lead: Twenty-eight competencies across seven domains, crossed by three threads. Move the level selector to read, across the entire map, what each competency means at that level of mastery.
framework.reminder: A reminder: this map describes a territory, not a pathway. Nobody is expected to master the whole, and there is no imposed order of progression.
framework.threadsLead: The threads do not add to the twenty-eight competencies: they qualify the way all of them are exercised. Discern, Sustain and Reinvent run through the seven domains the way ethics, endurance and adaptability run through any practice.

foundations.title: Grounding, principles and method
foundations.lead: What the framework describes, the principles it rests on, how it is organised and how it is assessed.

sections.title: Digital creative literacy
body: Digital creative literacy is the body of knowledge, know-how and dispositions that allows a person to critically receive, understand, imagine, make, publish and capitalise on content and projects in digital environments — autonomously, ethically and sustainably.

As reading, writing and arithmetic were to the civilisation of print, it constitutes a foundation: a body of knowledge society has an interest in seeing widely shared, and which can be mapped, observed and measured by levels — without anyone being expected to master all of it. CreaComp is that map.

sections.title: The thesis: an integrated architecture
body: CreaComp offers an integrated framework describing a person's capacity to understand digital environments, to create in them intentionally, to turn ideas into finished work, to engage with communities and to build lasting autonomy around what they make.

Taken on its own, none of these dimensions is unprecedented, and the framework does not claim otherwise. Searching for and evaluating information, understanding platforms and artificial intelligence, creativity, digital production, collaboration, audience building, running projects, entrepreneurship, intellectual property and value creation are already described elsewhere — by DigComp, by EntreComp, by media and information literacy, by research on creativity, by various models of digital competence.

What is original in CreaComp lies in its overall architecture rather than in any of its components taken separately. It gathers into one model, with a common grammar of levels and consistent evidence of assessment, dimensions that are usually studied and assessed apart from one another. That integration is the defensible claim, and it is what empirical validation has to put to the test.

sections.title: From the attention economy to the intention economy
body: The dominant digital economy captures attention: it optimises time spent, reflexive engagement, consumption endured rather than chosen. CreaComp argues for a shift: from an attention economy, in which people are the extracted resource, to an intention economy, in which they become authors again — of what they read, what they create and what they build.

Every domain of the framework can be reread through that shift: understanding algorithms not in order to flatter them but in order to choose what you feed; building a community you own rather than an audience you rent; creating with AI by directing it, rather than by delegating your judgement to it.

sections.title: The creator era and the displacement of value
body: Generative artificial intelligence has collapsed the cost of production: a competent text, a clean visual, an edited video are becoming universally accessible. What becomes ordinary loses its value; value moves towards both ends of the creative chain. Upstream: the eye — knowing what to create, why, and from which point of view. Downstream: the relationship — trust, community, and the ability to turn attention received into assets owned.

This reading does not change the architecture of the framework, which remains a complete map; it is its reading key. It explains why the upstream domains (Gather, Analyse, Create) and the downstream ones (Collaborate, Monetise) weigh as much as making itself.

items.title: A map, not a curriculum
items.body: CreaComp describes knowledge and makes it assessable; it prescribes no pathway, no method and no training content. Any instructional design can build on it; none follows from it automatically.

items.title: Universal entry
items.body: Every competency is accessible at Discovery level to a lower-secondary student equipped with nothing more than a smartphone. This is the framework's calibration golden rule: no level-1 descriptor presupposes professional equipment, an existing audience or an established activity.

items.title: Nobody is expected to master everything
items.body: The framework maps a territory; each person draws their own profile within it. There is no hierarchy between domains and no imposed order of progression: the same individual can be expert in one competency and a beginner in another.

items.title: Observable descriptors
items.body: Every level of every competency is described by what the person is able to do, verifiable by a third-party assessor, and paired with concrete evidence of assessment. The framework measures neither intentions nor isolated declarative knowledge.

items.title: Evidence of creation, never questionnaires
items.body: A framework for creators is assessed through artefacts: published content, completed projects, systems built, accompanied by a reflective analysis. The portfolio of evidence is the central instrument of validation.

items.title: Longevity through judgement
items.body: No descriptor names a piece of software, a platform or a model: the framework describes capacities of judgement, direction and method, which outlive the permanent renewal of tools.

items.title: A deliberately narrow scope
items.body: CreaComp deals with the creative side and mixes nothing else into it: account security, defensive personal-data protection and office software are deliberately excluded. Those belong to a general digital literacy, which this framework assumes in order to go further than it.

architecture.title: The architecture
body: The framework is organised into seven domains of action — named with verbs — each gathering four competencies, and crossed by three transversal threads. Every competency is described at four levels, giving 124 observable descriptors (28 competencies and 3 threads, multiplied by 4 levels), each paired with evidence of assessment.

levels.title: The grammar of the four levels
body: The levels describe postures, not ages: they apply identically to all competencies, which is what gives the framework its internal coherence. The educational landmarks are indicative.
levels.goldenRule: Golden rule: every Discovery-level descriptor is achievable by a lower-secondary student equipped with nothing more than a smartphone. This rule guarantees that the framework genuinely covers all audiences, from school to professional practice.

items.title: Evidence of creation
items.body: A competency is validated at a given level when the person produces the corresponding evidence of assessment — a real artefact: published content, a completed project, a system built, a written analysis — accompanied by a short reflective analysis (what I did, why, what I take from it), and when that evidence is verified by a third-party assessor against the descriptor. Validating a level entails validating the lower levels of the same competency.

items.title: The portfolio
items.body: The central instrument is the portfolio of evidence: a single artefact can attest to several competencies — a published video series can prove 3.3, 4.1 and 4.4 at once — and the portfolio draws the person's literacy profile: never an overall score, always an individual map. The framework produces neither average nor aggregate grade: adding up heterogeneous competencies would make no sense.

items.title: Validity requirements
items.body: To support scientific and certifying use, assessment based on CreaComp meets three requirements: verifiability (every descriptor is observable in the evidence produced, without extensive interpretation), inter-rater reliability (two trained assessors reach the same verdict on the same evidence) and traceability (each validation references the evidence, the date and the assessor). The framework is subject to an empirical validation protocol — a pilot study on real cohorts, measurement of inter-rater agreement, annual revision of ambiguous descriptors — as a precondition to any certifying claim.

perimeter.title: Scope: what CreaComp leaves out
body: CreaComp is a new framework, built on an object of its own: digital creative literacy. It neither extends nor subordinates itself to an existing framework. The European competence frameworks — DigComp for the digital competence of citizens, EntreComp for entrepreneurial competence — were its inspiration and its working basis, and they remain its natural complement. The overlaps with them are real and acknowledged: what sets CreaComp apart is not that it covers dimensions nobody has described, but that it articulates them within a single model.

What CreaComp deliberately leaves out, it leaves out as a matter of scope, not by deferring to an outside authority. It covers neither device and account security, nor defensive personal-data protection, nor technical problem-solving, nor office software and administrative communication. Those belong to a general digital literacy that is well served elsewhere, and duplicating them would have diluted the point. CreaComp assumes them available and deals exclusively with the creative side: understanding systems, conceiving, making, addressing, venturing, capitalising.

Three points of contact with general digital literacy deserve to be made explicit, because CreaComp goes further than it does at each. Competency 1.2 (reliability and manipulation) pushes critical reading as far as detecting synthetic content and the influence techniques specific to creative spaces. Competency 5.3 (conduct online) reaches moderation and the public handling of criticism. Competency 7.4 (platform-independent assets) treats data as property — owning your audience and your work — where the usual defensive approach stops at protecting it.

Finally, media and information literacy — a formal part of the French school curriculum — finds its natural extension in the Gather domain: CreaComp offers MIL teachers a trajectory leading from critical reception, their territory, towards assumed creation, which is its own.

profiles.title: Four ways to put it to work

items.name: Teach
items.body: Anchor a lesson sequence, a yearly progression or a class project in observable descriptors. The Discovery level is calibrated to be reachable with nothing more than a smartphone, which makes the framework usable from lower secondary onwards.
items.how: Select the relevant competencies, fix the target level, and have the associated evidence of assessment produced.

items.name: Train and certify
items.body: Build a legible training offer aligned with a public, citable framework, and assess it through evidence of creation. The validity requirements — verifiability, inter-rater reliability, traceability — are set out in the foundations.
items.how: Map your offer onto the 31 entries, then define the target exit level for each.

items.name: Locate yourself
items.body: A creator, a freelancer or a team can use the map as a mirror: where am I expert, where am I a beginner, which blind spot deserves work now.
items.how: Walk through the map level by level and spot the competencies where your actual practice falls short.

items.name: Research and inform policy
items.body: The framework is open, dated and citable. It lends itself to analysis, to comparison with other frameworks, to national or sectoral adaptation, and to reasoned criticism.
items.how: Cite the version and the edition, and flag your adaptations: they enrich the commons.

notPrescriptive.title: What the framework does not prescribe
notPrescriptive.body: CreaComp prescribes no pathway, no method, no training content, no duration and no tool. It defines no threshold for entering the labour market and produces no overall grade. Any instructional design can build on it; none follows from it automatically. This reserve is not false modesty: it is the condition for one framework to serve a secondary school, a vocational training provider and an independent creator without betraying any of them.

method.title: Hybrid work, and why say so
body: CreaComp was conceived by a human intelligence and composed with the help of artificial ones. The intention, the stances and the judgement calls come from an author; the shaping, part of the wording, the translation and the building of this site owe a great deal to generative systems, which made it possible to move faster and aim wider than wholly solitary work would have allowed.

What cannot be delegated stayed human: deciding what deserves to be a competence, placing the boundary between two levels, owning what the framework leaves out, and answering for every descriptor to those who will use it to teach or assess. A machine proposes and accelerates; it does not answer for the result. The author alone remains accountable for what CreaComp says.

Saying so is not a precaution, it is a matter of consistency. Competency 4.3 calls for creating with artificial intelligence through a “reasoned choice of what is delegated and what stays human”, and the Discern thread calls for creating “transparently, fairly and without manipulation”. A framework demanding of creators a transparency it does not apply to itself would be worth little.

It is, finally, what CreaComp argues for: conducted with discernment, hybridisation does not impoverish the work, it raises its ambition. It still has to be conducted well — which is precisely what this framework seeks to make teachable.
